scope: Vanda orchids, Nuwara Eliya highland region, Sri Lanka
_readme: Rule-based treatment knowledge base keyed by (disease, severity).
This is NOT a model. It is a lookup table, and that is a deliberate design
decision: treatment advice must be auditable and correctable by a human
expert, and there is no dataset of treatment outcomes to train on.
IMPORTANT -- FIELDS MARKED "VERIFY" ARE NOT YET SOURCED.
Cultural and sanitation practices below are standard, well-established
orchid husbandry. Chemical DOSAGES and SPRAY INTERVALS are deliberately
left as "VERIFY" rather than filled with plausible-looking numbers,
because prescribing an unverified agrochemical rate is unsafe and would be
indefensible in a viva. Fill each one from:
1. the product label of the formulation actually sold in Sri Lanka, and
2. the Department of Agriculture / Office of the Registrar of Pesticides
Then set "verified": true and record the page or URL in "source_ref".
Anything still marked VERIFY at submission time must be shown to the user
as 'consult your agricultural extension officer for application rates',

grading_protocol.basis: percentage of leaf area showing lesions, chlorosis or necrosis
grading_protocol.note: Graded by measured area rather than impression, so that labels stay consistent across all 427 diseased images. State this protocol in the report.

always_show: Read the product label before mixing. The label is the legal instruction.
Wear gloves, mask and eye protection when mixing or spraying.
Observe the pre-harvest and re-entry interval printed on the label.
Do not spray in direct midday sun or when temperature is above 30 C -- Vanda leaves scorch.
Test any new product on two or three plants and wait seven days before treating a whole collection.
safety.resistance_management: Rotate between fungicide groups with different FRAC codes. Using one active ingredient repeatedly selects for resistant strains and the product stops working.

sources.citation: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka -- floriculture crop protection guidance
sources.status: TO CITE -- add the exact publication, year and page

sources.citation: Orchid pest and disease reference used in this project
sources.status: TO CITE -- add author, title, year, page numbers

sources.citation: Reference-book chemical recommendations may predate current registrations. Where a modern alternative exists it is listed and flagged.

black_leaf_spot.pathogen_note: Confirm the causal organism with the research institute before publishing a species name. Several fungi produce visually similar black lesions on Vanda, and naming the wrong one in the report is an easy correction to be caught on.
black_leaf_spot.favourable_conditions: Prolonged leaf wetness, crowded plants, poor air movement, overhead watering late in the day.

mild.summary: A few small lesions. Cultural correction is usually enough; no spraying needed yet.
immediate_actions: Cut off affected leaf sections with a blade sterilised in flame or 70% alcohol.
Sterilise the blade again before moving to the next plant -- an unsterilised blade spreads infection faster than the fungus does.
Bag and destroy the removed material. Do not compost it near the collection.
Move the plant to a better-ventilated position and isolate it for two weeks.
cultural_control: Water at the base early in the day so leaves dry before nightfall.
Increase spacing so leaves of neighbouring plants do not touch.
Dust cut surfaces with cinnamon powder as a mild natural antifungal.

chemical_control.rationale: At under 10% leaf area, sanitation plus improved airflow normally halts spread. Spraying at this stage adds cost and selects for resistance without adding benefit.

mild.monitoring: Re-inspect every 3 days for 2 weeks. If new lesions appear, treat as moderate.

moderate.summary: Established infection spreading across the leaf. Sanitation plus a protectant fungicide.
immediate_actions: Isolate the plant from the collection immediately.
Remove all affected leaf tissue, cutting into healthy tissue beyond the lesion margin.
Sterilise tools between every cut.
Destroy removed material away from the growing area.
cultural_control: Stop overhead watering entirely until the infection is controlled.
Improve air movement -- a slow-moving fan is more effective than opening more vents.
Reduce humidity at night, which is when leaf wetness persists longest.
Check that pots and mounts drain freely.

chemical_control.rationale: Protects the healthy tissue that remains and stops lesion expansion.

options.notes: Broad-spectrum protectant with low resistance risk. Protects uninfected tissue; it does not cure established lesions.
Systemic, so it reaches tissue a spray cannot coat. FRAC group 1 has a known resistance history -- do not use it alone repeatedly.

moderate.monitoring: Re-inspect every 3 days. Keep the plant isolated until no new lesions appear for 2 weeks.

severe.summary: Over 40% of leaf area lost. The plant is at risk; treat aggressively and consider whether it is worth saving.
immediate_actions: Isolate immediately and well away from healthy plants.
Inspect every other plant in the collection -- at this severity, spread has usually already happened.
Remove all badly affected leaves even if this leaves the plant sparse.
If the crown or stem is involved, the prognosis is poor; consider destroying the plant to protect the collection.
cultural_control: Stop overhead watering completely.
Maximise air movement and reduce night humidity.
Do not fertilise heavily -- soft new growth is more susceptible.
Repot into fresh medium only after the infection is under control, not during.

chemical_control.rationale: A systemic product is needed; a protectant alone cannot reach infection already inside the tissue.

options.notes: Modern combination product. Two modes of action in one formulation slow resistance development. Confirm it is registered for ornamentals in Sri Lanka before recommending it to a grower.
Alternate with a different FRAC group between applications.

severe.monitoring: Inspect every 2 days. If lesions continue spreading after two full applications, stop and seek expert diagnosis -- the causal organism may have been misidentified.
severe.escalation_reason: At this severity a wrong diagnosis is costly, and continued spread after treatment suggests the pathogen is not what was assumed.

phyllosticta_leaf_spot.favourable_conditions: Warm, consistently humid conditions with water sitting on leaves. Spores spread in splashing water, so overhead irrigation is the main vector.
phyllosticta_leaf_spot.distinguishing_note: Lesions typically begin as small purple-black flecks that enlarge into elongated sunken spots, often with a yellow halo, running along the leaf axis.

mild.summary: Scattered small flecks. Correct the watering and airflow before reaching for chemicals.
immediate_actions: Trim affected leaf tips or sections with a sterilised blade.
Sterilise between cuts and between plants.
Destroy the removed tissue.
Isolate the plant for observation.
cultural_control: Switch to base watering. Splashing water is how this spreads.
Water early enough that leaves are dry before dark.
Increase spacing and air movement.
Dust cut surfaces with cinnamon powder.

chemical_control.rationale: Under 10% leaf area, cultural correction alone usually stops it. Spraying here trains resistance without a benefit to show for it.

moderate.summary: Lesions coalescing and spreading. Sanitation plus a protectant or systemic fungicide.
immediate_actions: Isolate the plant.
Remove affected tissue, cutting beyond the lesion margin into healthy tissue.
Sterilise tools between cuts.
Check neighbouring plants -- splash spread means the nearest plants are most at risk.
cultural_control: Stop overhead watering entirely.
Improve air circulation with gentle continuous movement.
Lower night-time humidity.
Avoid heavy nitrogen feeding while the infection is active.

chemical_control.rationale: Protects remaining healthy tissue and limits new infection sites.

options.notes: Low resistance risk, good rotation partner.
Check current registration status for ornamentals in Sri Lanka -- registrations for this active ingredient have changed in several countries.

moderate.monitoring: Re-inspect every 3 days; keep isolated until 2 weeks pass with no new lesions.

severe.summary: Extensive leaf loss. Systemic treatment, and reassess whether the plant is worth keeping.
immediate_actions: Isolate well away from the collection.
Inspect the entire collection -- assume spread has already occurred.
Remove all heavily affected leaves.
If the crown is affected, consider destroying the plant.
cultural_control: No overhead watering under any circumstances.
Maximise airflow; reduce night humidity.
Hold off on fertiliser until recovery is under way.
Do not repot while the infection is active.

chemical_control.rationale: Established internal infection needs a systemic product with more than one mode of action.

options.notes: Modern option, more effective than older reference-book recommendations for this pathogen. Confirm ornamental registration in Sri Lanka.
Effective but resistance-prone. Alternate FRAC groups between applications.
Rotation partner. Do not follow with another group 11 product.

severe.monitoring: Inspect every 2 days. No improvement after two applications means the diagnosis should be re-examined.
severe.escalation_reason: Severe cases justify expert confirmation of the pathogen before further chemical use.

none.summary: No disease detected. Advice here is preventive maintenance.
immediate_actions: No treatment needed. Do not spray fungicide preventively on a healthy plant -- it costs money and builds resistance for no benefit.
cultural_control: Water at the base in the morning so leaves are dry by nightfall.
Keep plants spaced so leaves do not touch.
Maintain steady gentle air movement.
Sterilise cutting tools between plants as routine practice, not just when disease appears.
Quarantine any newly acquired plant for 3 to 4 weeks before adding it to the collection.

chemical_control.rationale: Preventive spraying of healthy plants selects for resistant pathogen strains and offers no measurable benefit at collection scale.

none.monitoring: Inspect weekly, paying attention to leaf undersides and the crown where early lesions are easiest to miss.

unidentified._note: Returned when the classifier's highest softmax probability falls below the operating threshold. There is no trained 'other' class -- there were not enough images of any fourth condition to train one. This entry exists so the system never names a disease it cannot advise on.

unknown.summary: The plant does not appear healthy, but the system is not confident enough to name the condition. Do not treat on a guess.
immediate_actions: Isolate the plant from the rest of the collection as a precaution.
Photograph the affected area clearly in daylight, including a whole-plant shot for context.
Do not apply any chemical until the condition is identified -- the wrong product wastes money, can damage the plant, and can make a correct later diagnosis harder.
Contact an agricultural extension officer or the orchid research institute with the photographs.
cultural_control: Reduce leaf wetness and improve airflow. These help against almost every foliar problem and harm nothing.
Withhold fertiliser until the cause is known.

chemical_control.rationale: Treating an unidentified condition is guessing. If the cause is an oomycete such as Phytophthora rather than a true fungus, standard fungicides will not work at all.

unknown.monitoring: Photograph daily to record progression -- a clear progression sequence greatly helps an expert diagnose it.
unknown.escalation_reason: Low classifier confidence means the condition is outside the three trained classes, or the photograph is unclear.

invalid_image._note: Returned when the input validator decides the photograph is not a Vanda orchid at all -- food, a hand, a table, a building, a different plant. This is NOT the same as 'unidentified'. Unidentified means the image IS an orchid whose condition the model cannot name, and the right advice is to consult an expert. Invalid means the wrong subject was photographed, and the right advice is to take another photo. Wording them the same would send a grower to an expert over a picture of their lunch.

none.summary: This does not look like a Vanda orchid, so no diagnosis was attempted.
immediate_actions: Photograph a single Vanda orchid leaf or stem.
Fill most of the frame with the leaf -- step closer rather than zooming.
Use daylight or bright shade; avoid direct midday sun and deep shadow.
Hold the camera steady and check the photo is in focus before uploading.
cultural_control: Photograph the affected part directly rather than the whole plant.
Keep other plants, pots and hands out of the frame where possible.

chemical_control.rationale: No plant was identified, so no treatment can be suggested. Nothing should be applied on the basis of this image.

none.monitoring: Retake the photograph and analyse it again.

_note: Not produced by the classifier -- these three classes were dropped for lack of training images.
Kept in the knowledge base for two reasons: the admin can enter these diagnoses manually,
and the Phytophthora distinction below is a genuine trap that the report should record.

phytophthora_black_rot.critical_note: Phytophthora is an OOMYCETE (water mould), NOT a true fungus. Its cell walls are cellulose rather than chitin, so most standard fungicides -- mancozeb, thiophanate-methyl, the strobilurins -- have little or no effect on it. This distinction is the single most important thing in this file: treating black rot with an ordinary fungicide loses the plant while appearing to be doing something.

correct_chemical_classes.notes: Systemic, moves both up and down the plant.
Soil and medium drench for root and crown infection.

phytophthora_black_rot.natural_option: Cinnamon powder or cinnamon paste applied to cut surfaces is a widely used natural treatment among orchid growers, appropriate for small lesions and for sealing cuts after removing rotted tissue.
cultural_control: Reduce water immediately -- this organism needs free water to spread.
Improve drainage and air movement.
Cut well beyond the rot margin into clean tissue; the rot front runs ahead of the visible discolouration.
Isolate and inspect neighbours; spread through shared water is rapid.

anthracnose.status: Out of scope for the classifier. 791 images exist from an earlier collection but the class was excluded when scope narrowed to three classes on 29 Aug 2026.
anthracnose.note: If reinstated, it needs its own treatment entry filled in before the classifier is allowed to predict it -- otherwise the system names a disease it cannot advise on.

sooty_mold.status: Out of scope for the classifier.
sooty_mold.note: Sooty mold grows on honeydew excreted by sap-sucking insects. It is a SYMPTOM, not the primary problem -- controlling the insects (scale, mealybug, aphid) removes the cause. Treating the mold alone achieves nothing lasting.
